title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: It was eight o'clock when we landed. We walked briefly along the shore, enjoying the fading light, then retired to the inn. We looked out at the lovely scene of water, woods, and mountains, growing dark yet still showing their black outlines.

The wind, which had died in the south, now rose violently from the west. The moon had reached its peak and was beginning to descend. Clouds swept across it faster than the flight of a vulture, dimming its rays. The lake reflected the turbulent sky, made even more restless by waves that were starting to build. A heavy rain suddenly descended.

I'd been calm during the day, but as soon as darkness hid the shapes of things, a thousand fears filled my mind. I was anxious and watchful. My right hand gripped a pistol hidden inside my coat. Every sound terrified me. But I resolved to sell my life dearly and not shrink from the fight until either my own life or my enemy's was ended.
Elizabeth watched my agitation in frightened silence. Then something in my glance communicated my terror to her. Trembling, she asked, "What's troubling you, my dear Victor? What are you afraid of?"
"Oh! Peace, peace, my love," I replied. "After tonight, all will be safe. But tonight is dreadful — truly dreadful."

I spent an hour in this state, then suddenly realized how terrifying the combat would be for my wife. I begged her to go to bed, planning not to join her until I'd learned something about my enemy's whereabouts.

She left me. I continued pacing the halls, inspecting every corner where my enemy might hide. But I found no trace of him. I was beginning to think some lucky chance had prevented him from carrying out his threat — when I suddenly heard a shrill, terrible scream. It came from the room where Elizabeth had gone. As I heard it, the whole truth rushed into my mind. My arms dropped. Every muscle froze. I could feel blood trickling through my veins and tingling in my fingertips. This state lasted only an instant. The scream was repeated. I ran to the room.

Great God! Why didn't I die at that moment? Why am I here to describe the destruction of the best hope and purest creature on earth? She was there — lifeless and still — thrown across the bed, her head hanging down, her pale, twisted features half covered by her hair. Everywhere I look, I see the same image: her bloodless arms and limp body flung by the murderer onto her bridal bier. Could I see this and live? Alas! Life is stubborn. It clings tightest where it's most unwanted. For just a moment I lost consciousness and fell to the ground.

When I revived, I found myself surrounded by the inn's staff. Their faces showed breathless terror, but their horror seemed like a shadow, a mockery, compared to what I felt. I escaped from them to the room where Elizabeth's body lay — my love, my wife, so recently alive, so dear, so worthy. She'd been moved from the position I first saw her in. Now, as she lay with her head resting on her arm and a handkerchief across her face and neck, I might have thought her asleep. I rushed to her and embraced her passionately. But the deathly limpness and coldness of her limbs told me that what I held in my arms was no longer the Elizabeth I had loved and cherished. The murderous mark of the fiend's grip was on her neck. Her breath had stopped.

While I still hung over her in agony, I happened to look up. The windows had been darkened before, and I felt a kind of panic when I saw the pale yellow light of the moon lighting up the room. The shutters had been thrown back. With a horror I can't describe, I saw at the open window a figure of the most hideous, loathsome kind. A grin was on the monster's face. He seemed to sneer as, with his fiendish finger, he pointed at my wife's corpse. I rushed to the window and drew a pistol from my coat. I fired. But he dodged me, leaped from the windowsill, and running with the speed of lightning, plunged into the lake.

The gunshot brought a crowd into the room. I pointed to the spot where he'd disappeared. We followed in boats. Nets were cast. But it was hopeless. After searching for several hours, we returned. Most of my companions believed the figure had been a product of my imagination. Once we had landed, they went on to search the countryside, splitting into parties that went in different directions among the woods and vineyards.

I tried to go with the search parties, walking a short distance from the house. But my head spun. My steps were like a drunk man's. I finally collapsed in a state of complete exhaustion. A film covered my eyes. My skin burned with fever. In this condition I was carried back and put to bed, barely aware of what had happened. My eyes wandered around the room as if searching for something lost.

After a while I got up and, as if by instinct, crawled to the room where my beloved's body lay. Women were weeping around it. I hung over the body and joined my tears to theirs. No clear thought formed in my mind — just confused reflections on my misfortunes and their cause. I was bewildered, lost in a cloud of horror and wonder. The death of William, the execution of Justine, the murder of Clerval, and now of my wife — even at that moment I didn't know whether my remaining family was safe from the fiend's malice. My father might even now be writhing in his grasp. Ernest might be dead at his feet. This thought made me shudder and jolted me into action. I resolved to return to Geneva with all possible speed.

No horses could be found. I would have to cross the lake, but the wind was against us and rain poured in torrents. Still, it was barely morning. I could reasonably hope to arrive by nightfall. I hired rowers and took an oar myself — I had always found relief from mental anguish in physical effort. But the overwhelming grief I now felt made me incapable of any real exertion. I dropped the oar. Leaning my head on my hands, I gave way to every dark thought. If I looked up, I saw scenes that were familiar from my happier days — scenes I'd admired just yesterday in the company of the woman who was now only a shadow and a memory. Tears streamed from my eyes. The rain stopped for a moment, and I saw the fish playing in the water as they had a few hours before, when Elizabeth had watched them. Nothing is so painful as a great and sudden change. The sun might shine or clouds might gather, but nothing could look to me as it had the day before. A fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness. No creature had ever been so miserable as I was. This event stands alone in the history of human suffering.

But why should I dwell on what followed? Mine has been a tale of horrors. I've reached their peak. What I must now relate can only be tedious to you. Know that, one by one, my friends were torn from me. I was left utterly alone. My own strength is gone. I must tell what remains of my hideous story in a few words.

I reached Geneva. My father and Ernest were still alive. But my father collapsed under the news I brought. I see him now — that excellent, noble old man! His eyes wandered vacantly. They had lost their light — Elizabeth, his more than daughter, whom he loved with all the devotion a man feels in the twilight of life, when few attachments remain and he clings all the more tightly to those that do. Cursed, cursed be the fiend that brought misery to his gray hairs and doomed him to waste away in wretchedness! He couldn't bear the horrors accumulating around him. The springs of his life suddenly gave way. He couldn't rise from his bed. Within a few days, he died in my arms.

What became of me after that? I don't know. I lost all sensation. Chains and darkness were the only things I was aware of. Sometimes I dreamed of wandering through flowery meadows with the friends of my youth. But I always woke to find myself in a dungeon. Depression followed. Gradually I gained a clear understanding of my situation and was released from prison — for they had declared me mad, and for many months, as I understood it, a solitary cell had been my home.

Freedom would have been a worthless gift if I hadn't also awakened to revenge. As memories of past horrors pressed on me, I began to think about their cause — the monster I had created, the wretched demon I had sent into the world to destroy me. A maddening rage consumed me whenever I thought of him. I prayed desperately for the chance to get my hands on him and wreak a great and memorable revenge on his cursed head.

My hatred didn't confine itself to useless wishes for long. I began to think about the best way to capture him, and for this purpose, about a month after my release, I went to a criminal judge in the town. I told him I had an accusation to make — that I knew who had destroyed my family — and asked him to use his full authority to apprehend the murderer.
The magistrate listened with attention and kindness. "Be assured, sir," he said, "I will spare no effort to discover the villain."

"Thank you," I replied. "Listen, then, to the statement I have to make. It's a story so strange that I'd expect you not to believe it — if there weren't something in truth which, however incredible, compels conviction. The story is too coherent to be mistaken for a dream, and I have no reason to lie." My manner was controlled but impressive. I had formed in my heart a resolution to pursue my destroyer to the death. This purpose quieted my anguish and briefly reconciled me to life. I then told my story briefly but firmly, marking the dates accurately and never breaking into outrage or exclamation.

The magistrate seemed completely incredulous at first. But as I continued, he became more attentive and interested. I saw him sometimes shudder with horror. At other times, a lively surprise — with no trace of disbelief — appeared on his face.

When I'd finished, I said, "This is the being I accuse. I call upon you to use your full power to capture and punish him. It is your duty as a magistrate, and I trust your human feelings won't revolt at carrying it out."

This request caused a considerable change in the magistrate's expression. He'd been listening with the half-belief people give to tales of ghosts and the supernatural. But when called upon to take official action, his skepticism returned in full. He answered mildly, "I would gladly help you pursue this creature. But the being you describe seems to have powers that would defeat all my efforts. Who can chase an animal that crosses the sea of ice and hides in caves where no man would dare go? Besides, months have passed since his crimes. No one can guess where he's gone or where he might be now."

"I'm sure he's hovering near the spot where I live. If he has taken refuge in the Alps, he can be hunted like a mountain goat and killed like a beast of prey. But I can see what you're thinking. You don't believe my story and don't intend to pursue my enemy with the punishment he deserves."

As I spoke, rage flashed in my eyes. The magistrate was intimidated. "You're mistaken," he said. "I will do everything I can. If it's possible to catch the monster, I assure you he'll be punished according to his crimes. But from what you've described of his abilities, I fear it will prove impossible. And while every proper step is taken, you should prepare yourself for disappointment."

"That cannot be. But anything I say will be useless. My revenge means nothing to you. Yet while I admit it's a vice, I confess it's the consuming, sole passion of my soul. My rage is unspeakable when I think that the murderer I let loose still exists. You refuse my just demand. I have only one option. I devote myself — in life or in death — to his destruction."

I trembled with extreme agitation as I said this. There was a frenzy in my manner, and something, I don't doubt, of that haughty fierceness that martyrs of old are said to have possessed. But to a Geneva magistrate, whose mind was occupied by far different concerns than devotion and heroism, this intensity of feeling looked very much like madness. He tried to soothe me the way a nurse calms a child and treated my story as the product of delirium.
"Man," I cried, "how ignorant you are in your pride of wisdom! Stop. You don't know what you're saying."
I stormed from the house, angry and frustrated, and went away to plan some other course of action.
